query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The stability of equiatomic high‐entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles across catalytic and thermoelectric temperatures is governed by the balance between favorable configurational entropy and the differential surface energies of the constituent metals. When the differences in intrinsic surface energies are minimal, surface segregation is suppressed, maintaining a single-phase solid solution; in contrast, if one element has a substantially lower surface energy, it will segregate at elevated temperatures, leading to phase separation or oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios that are initially crystallized as a single‐phase solid solution.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled compositional deviation by slightly increasing (e.g., by a controlled, reproducible excess) the content of one metal known to have a significantly lower surface energy relative to the others. This intervention is compared against the baseline equiatomic composition.
generation.conditions: The nanoparticles are exposed to catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions over the temperature range of 473–1923 K in the same controlled reactive or inert atmosphere as specified in the baseline regime.
generation.structural_mediator: The extent of surface segregation and any resulting phase decomposition or oxidation, as revealed by high-resolution imaging (e.g., TEM, STEM-EDX) and surface-sensitive spectroscopy (e.g., XPS).
generation.mechanism: Differential surface energies drive atomic diffusion at high temperatures. In the baseline equiatomic state, similar surface energies minimize elemental segregation and maintain the solid solution phase. In the intervention sample, the increased proportion of the low surface energy element enhances surface segregation, creating a distinct surface layer that either passivates (if beneficial) or leads to destabilization via phase separation or oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the same high-temperature operating conditions, the baseline equiatomic nanoparticles will largely maintain their single-phase solid solution structure with minimal measurable surface segregation, while the intervention sample (with the enriched low-surface-energy element) will exhibit measurable surface segregation and early signs of phase decomposition or oxidation relative to baseline.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic high-entropy alloy nanoparticles initially in a single‐phase solid solution state.
generation.boundary: Observations are restricted to the operating temperature range of 473–1923 K under the same catalytic or thermoelectric test environment.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold at which the difference in surface energy leads to significant segregation, as well as the quantitative extent of any phase decomposition or oxidation, is uncertain and may vary with specific element choices and operational atmospheres.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of nanoparticles: (1) control nanoparticles with an ideal equiatomic five-or-more-metal composition and (2) a modified set where one metal (with a lower inherent surface energy) is present at a slightly elevated concentration. Subject both sets to identical catalytic/thermoelectric testing conditions across 473–1923 K in a controlled atmosphere. After exposure, analyze both sets using high-resolution TEM/STEM-EDX for phase mapping and XPS for surface composition.
measurements: Phase homogeneity and segregation analysis by (S)TEM-EDX
Detection and quantification of any secondary phases or oxide formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the equiatomic control and the modified nanoparticles show no significant difference in surface composition, phase homogeneity, or onset of oxidation/decomposition after high-temperature treatment, then the role of differential surface energy in governing stability is not supported, thereby falsifying the hypothesis.
